title: Goulash
subtitle: Hungarian beef and paprika stew
excerpt: Beef braised low and slow with a large quantity of sweet paprika, onions, and caraway seeds in a thick, dark sauce. The national dish of Hungary, earthy and warming.

recipe.sourceNotes: Goulash (gulyás in Hungarian) is the national dish of Hungary, originally a herdsman's stew of beef, onions, and paprika cooked over an open fire in a kettle (bogrács). Paprika, made from dried red peppers, was not introduced to Hungary until the 16th or 17th century, but the dish evolved to depend on it so fundamentally that it is now inseparable from Hungarian cooking. The authentic version uses only beef, onion, paprika, caraway, and stock: no tomatoes, no peppers, no cream. The British and American version often includes these, producing a thicker, sweeter, and heavier stew. This recipe follows the more restrained Hungarian original.

recipeTools.notes: Heavy casserole dish for the long braise.

content.text: The paprika is the whole flavour base of this dish. Use a large quantity of sweet Hungarian paprika, not hot paprika and not smoked paprika, which are different things. Add it off the heat or on a very low flame: paprika burns easily and turns bitter. The onions must be cooked down to a complete softness before the paprika goes in. Do not rush the braise: goulash needs at least 1.5 to 2 hours for the beef to fully tenderise.
Heat the oil in a heavy casserole over medium heat. Cook the onions for 20 minutes until completely soft and golden, stirring often. Add the garlic and cook for 2 minutes.
Remove from the heat. Add the paprika, caraway, marjoram, and tomato puree. Stir well. Return to a low heat and stir for 1 minute. Do not let the paprika burn.

Add the beef and stir to coat in the paprika mixture. Add the stock and bay leaves. Season with salt and pepper. Bring to a simmer, cover, and cook on the lowest heat for 1.5 to 2 hours until the beef is completely tender and the sauce has thickened. Stir occasionally and add a splash of water if it looks dry.
Remove the bay leaves. Taste and adjust seasoning. Serve with egg noodles or bread dumplings, topped with a spoonful of soured cream.
